questions.stem: What is the back emf in a DC electric motor?
options: An emf produced by the brushes when the commutator reverses the current
An emf induced in the rotating coil that opposes the supply voltage
An emf from the supply that drives current backwards through the coil
An emf induced in the magnets that adds to the supply voltage
questions.explanation: As the coil rotates in the magnetic field it cuts flux, so it acts as a generator and an emf is induced in it. By Lenz's law this emf opposes the change that causes it, so it acts against the supply voltage. It is induced in the coil, not the magnets, and it is present whenever the coil turns.

questions.stem: Which law explains why the back emf in a motor opposes the supply voltage rather than adding to it?
options: Ohm's law, which relates the current to the resistance
Coulomb's law, which describes the force between charges
Newton's third law, which pairs the forces on the coil
Lenz's law, which follows from conservation of energy
questions.explanation: Lenz's law says an induced emf drives a current whose effects oppose the change producing it. If the back emf added to the supply, the motor would speed up without limit and create energy from nothing, which conservation of energy forbids. Ohm's law is used with the back emf, but it does not set its direction.

questions.stem: A DC motor is switched on from rest. How do its back emf and current change as it speeds up to its running speed?
options: The back emf rises and the current falls
The back emf falls and the current rises
Both the back emf and the current rise
Both stay constant once it is switched on
questions.explanation: The back emf is proportional to how fast the coil cuts flux, so it starts at zero and grows as the motor speeds up. The net emf driving current is the supply voltage minus the back emf, so the current is largest at switch-on and falls as the motor reaches speed.

questions.stem: A 12 V DC motor has a coil resistance of 2.0 Ω. When running at full speed it draws 1.5 A. What is the back emf?
questions.explanation: The net emf across the coil's resistance is V − ε = IR, so ε = 12 − 1.5 × 2.0 = 9.0 V. The 3.0 V answer is the voltage drop across the resistance, not the back emf, and 15 V adds the drop instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: The 12 V motor with a coil resistance of 2.0 Ω is switched on. What current flows at the instant it starts, before the coil has begun to turn?
questions.explanation: At rest the coil is not cutting flux, so there is no back emf and the full 12 V drives current through the 2.0 Ω coil: I = 12/2.0 = 6.0 A. This is four times the running current of 1.5 A, which is why motors draw a surge of current at switch-on.

questions.stem: A 240 V motor with a coil resistance of 4.0 Ω draws 5.0 A when running. At what rate is it doing mechanical work, ignoring friction?
options: 14 kW
1.1 kW
1.2 kW
questions.explanation: The back emf is 240 − 5.0 × 4.0 = 220 V, and the rate of mechanical work is the back emf times the current: 220 × 5.0 = 1.1 kW. The input power is 240 × 5.0 = 1.2 kW, and the other 0.10 kW, I²R, heats the coil. 14 kW comes from V²/R, which wrongly treats the whole 240 V as across the resistance.

questions.stem: A 12 V motor with a coil resistance of 0.60 Ω produces a back emf of 10.8 V when running freely. What current does it draw?
questions.explanation: The net emf driving current is 12 − 10.8 = 1.2 V, so I = 1.2/0.60 = 2.0 A. Using the full 12 V gives 20 A, the starting current, and using only the back emf gives 18 A. A small net emf is why a free-running motor draws little current.

questions.stem: A food processor's motor slows down when the blades meet a thick mixture. What happens to the current in the motor and why?
options: It decreases, because the slower coil cuts flux less often
It stays the same, because the supply voltage is unchanged
It decreases, because the extra load raises the coil's resistance
It increases, because the slower coil produces less back emf
questions.explanation: Slower rotation means the coil cuts flux more slowly, so the back emf falls. The net emf, supply voltage minus back emf, rises, and so does the current, giving more torque to drive the load. The coil's resistance is unaffected by the load.

questions.stem: A drill motor jams and stops turning while still switched on. Why is it in danger of burning out?
options: With no rotation, the commutator stops reversing the current
With no back emf, the supply voltage across the coil doubles
With no rotation, the coil's resistance drops to almost zero
With no back emf, a large current flows and heats the coil
questions.explanation: A stalled coil cuts no flux, so there is no back emf and the full supply voltage drives a large current through the low resistance of the coil. The heating, I²R, is then many times its normal value. The supply voltage itself does not change, and the resistance only rises slightly as the coil heats.

questions.stem: Large motors are often started with a resistor in series with the coil, which is switched out as the motor speeds up. What is the purpose of this resistor?
options: To limit the large starting current while the back emf is small
To increase the back emf so that the motor starts more quickly
To reverse the current in the coil every half turn of the motor
To store energy so the motor can keep turning if the supply fails
questions.explanation: At start-up there is little back emf to oppose the supply, so the current could be large enough to damage the coil or the supply. A series resistor limits it until the back emf has built up. The resistor does not create back emf, and current reversal is the commutator's job.

questions.stem: In an electric or hybrid car, what happens during regenerative braking?
options: The motor acts as a generator, converting kinetic energy to electrical energy
The brakes heat up and the heat is stored and later turned into electricity
The battery supplies current to the motor in reverse to push the car back
The motor is disconnected so the car slows by air resistance alone
questions.explanation: When the driver brakes, the wheels turn the motor's coil, which then acts as a generator. The induced current charges the battery, so some of the car's kinetic energy is stored instead of being lost as heat in friction brakes. No energy is drawn from the battery to slow the car.

questions.stem: During regenerative braking, why does the generated current slow the car down?
options: By Lenz's law, the induced current produces a force opposing the motion
The induced current increases the friction between the tyres and road
The battery's chemical energy is used to push against the wheels
The induced current heats the coil, and the heat resists the motion
questions.explanation: The induced current flows through the coil in the magnetic field, so the coil experiences a force. By Lenz's law that force opposes the rotation that produced the current, so the wheels are slowed. This is the same electromagnetic effect that makes a generator harder to turn when it supplies current.

questions.stem: A 1500 kg electric car slows from 20 m s⁻¹ to rest, and regenerative braking stores 60% of its kinetic energy in the battery. How much energy is stored?
questions.explanation: The kinetic energy is ½ × 1500 × 20² = 3.0 × 10⁵ J, and 60% of that is 1.8 × 10⁵ J. The 1.2 × 10⁵ J answer is the 40% that is not recovered, and 3.6 × 10⁵ J comes from using mv² without the ½.

questions.stem: A 1500 kg hybrid car slows from 25 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹, and 70% of the lost kinetic energy is stored by regenerative braking. How much energy is stored?
questions.explanation: The kinetic energy lost is ½ × 1500 × (25² − 10²) ≈ 3.9 × 10⁵ J, and 70% of that is about 2.8 × 10⁵ J. Using the change in speed, 70% of ½ × 1500 × 15², gives 1.2 × 10⁵ J, which is wrong because kinetic energy depends on v², not on Δv. The 3.9 × 10⁵ J answer is the total lost before taking 70%.

questions.stem: Why do electric cars still need friction brakes in addition to regenerative braking?
options: Regenerative braking can only be used when travelling uphill
The induced current flows the wrong way when the car slows down
The induced emf, and so the braking force, falls as the car slows
Regenerative braking only works while the car's battery is empty
questions.explanation: The induced emf depends on how fast the coil turns, so at low speeds the induced current and braking force become small and cannot hold the car still. Friction brakes are also needed for emergency stops and when the battery is full and cannot accept more charge.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why regenerative braking improves an electric car's driving range in city traffic?
options: Energy that friction brakes would waste as heat is returned to the battery
The motor uses less current to accelerate because the battery is cooler
The induced current increases the motor's back emf when it accelerates
The car's mass is reduced because it needs smaller friction brakes
questions.explanation: Each time a car stops, friction brakes turn its kinetic energy into heat that is lost. Regenerative braking returns part of that energy to the battery, to be used again for acceleration. Stop-start city driving involves many such stops, so the gain is largest there.

questions.stem: A car's motor is used as a generator for regenerative braking. Which change would increase the braking force at a given speed, if the coil and field are unchanged?
options: Drawing a larger current from the coil into the battery
Disconnecting the coil from the battery completely
Reducing the speed at which the wheels turn the coil
Reversing the direction in which the magnets are mounted
questions.explanation: The braking force comes from the force on the current-carrying coil in the field, F = IlB, so a larger induced current gives a larger opposing force. With the coil disconnected there is an emf but no current, and so no braking force. Reversing the magnets reverses the current too, so the force still opposes the motion.

questions.stem: How does an induction hotplate heat a saucepan?
options: A changing magnetic field induces eddy currents in the pan's base, which heat it
A hot coil under the glass top conducts heat up through the glass to the pan
Microwaves from the coil are absorbed by the water molecules in the food
A steady magnetic field magnetises the pan, and the magnetism produces heat
questions.explanation: Alternating current in a coil under the glass makes a rapidly changing magnetic field. The changing flux through the pan's base induces eddy currents in it (Faraday's law), and the resistance of the metal converts their energy into heat (I²R). The coil itself does not get hot like a conventional element.

questions.stem: Why must the current in an induction hotplate's coil be alternating rather than direct?
options: A direct current would magnetise the pan and pull it onto the glass
A direct current would heat the coil instead of the pan
A direct current cannot produce any magnetic field at all
A direct current gives a steady flux, which induces no emf in the pan
questions.explanation: Faraday's law says an emf is induced only when the flux changes. A direct current makes a steady field, so the flux through the pan does not change and no eddy currents flow. A direct current does produce a magnetic field; it just does not induce anything in a stationary pan.

questions.stem: During cooking on an induction hotplate, the glass top stays much cooler than the pan. Why?
options: Glass has a high specific heat capacity, so its temperature never rises
Glass is an electrical insulator, so no eddy currents flow in it
Glass reflects the magnetic field upward, away from its surface
Glass is a magnetic material, so it absorbs the changing field
questions.explanation: Eddy currents need a conductor. The glass-ceramic top does not conduct, so no current is induced in it and it is warmed only by contact with the hot pan. Glass is not magnetic and does not block or reflect the field, which passes through it to the pan.

questions.stem: A cook finds that a cast-iron pan heats well on an induction hotplate but a glass pan does not heat at all. What is the reason?
options: Glass is transparent, so it cannot absorb the energy from the coil
No eddy currents can be induced in glass, which does not conduct electricity
Glass is too thick for the magnetic field to reach the food inside
Glass has a higher melting point, so it absorbs the heat from the coil
questions.explanation: The pan is heated by currents induced in it, so it must conduct electricity. Glass does not, so no current flows and no heat is produced. Cast iron is a conductor and is also ferromagnetic, which concentrates the field in the base and makes heating effective.

questions.stem: In an induction hotplate, the field through a loop in a pan's base changes by 0.010 T in 5.0 µs. The loop has an area of 0.015 m². What average emf is induced around it?
questions.explanation: Faraday's law gives ε = ΔΦ/Δt = ΔB × A/Δt = 0.010 × 0.015/(5.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 30 V. The 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ V answer is the change in flux, which still needs dividing by the time. A rapid change in flux is why even a small field induces large eddy currents.

questions.stem: The frequency of the alternating current in an induction hotplate's coil is increased, with the peak field unchanged. How does this affect the heating of the pan?
options: Heating increases, because the faster-changing flux induces a larger emf
Heating decreases, because the field has less time to build up each cycle
Heating is unchanged, because the peak field strength is the same
Heating decreases, because eddy currents can only flow at low frequency
questions.explanation: By Faraday's law the induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux. With the same peak field, a higher frequency means the flux changes faster, so larger eddy currents flow and more heat is produced. This is why induction hotplates use frequencies far above the 50 Hz mains supply.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of an induction hotplate over a conventional electric element?
options: The heat is produced in the pan itself, so less energy is lost to the surroundings
The coil reaches a higher temperature than a conventional element, cooking faster
It needs no electrical supply, because the pan generates its own current
It heats any material placed on it, including glass and ceramic dishes
questions.explanation: In an induction hotplate the eddy currents heat the pan directly, so little energy goes into heating the cooktop and the air around it. A conventional element must first heat itself and then the pan. The induction coil stays relatively cool, and the hotplate only heats conducting pans.
